3.2.5.1-f29.text: Amantium morbus ut pruritus solvitur, venae sectione & cucurbitulis

translations.note: This sidenote backs up Burton's mention of bloodletting in the main text. It does not translate that text.
translations.text: The disease of lovers, like an itch, is relieved by bloodletting and cupping-glasses.

translations.note: Burton's English at the anchor mentions only bloodletting, so it is not a rendering of this sentence.

3.2.5.1-f31.text: ut Camphora pudendis alligata, & in bracha gestata (quidam ait) membrum flaccidum reddit. Laboravit hoc morbo virgo nobilis, cui inter caetera praescripsit Medicus, ut laminam plumbeam multis foraminibus pertusam ad dies viginti portaret in dorso; ad exiccandum vero sperma jussit eam quam parcissime cibari, & manducare frequenter coriandrum praeparatum, et semen lactucae et acetosae, et sic eam a morbo liberavit

translations.note: The passage starts in mid-sentence. The words just before it, 'Huc faciunt medicamenta Venerem sopientia', mean 'To this purpose serve medicines that lull Venus to sleep'. 'Bracha' stands for braca, 'breeches'. 'Acetosa' is sorrel. 'Sperma' in a woman reflects the Galenic belief in female seed.
translations.text: as camphor bound to the private parts and carried in the breeches (someone says) makes the member flaccid. A noble maiden laboured under this disease, for whom, among other things, the physician prescribed that she should wear on her back for twenty days a thin plate of lead pierced with many holes; and to dry up the seed he ordered that she be fed as sparingly as possible, and often eat prepared coriander, and the seed of lettuce and of sorrel, and so he freed her from the disease.

translations.note: The passage begins mid-sentence, after "Huc faciunt medicamenta Venerem sopientia," so "ut" is rendered "as". "f." is read as fiat ("make"), and "Nenupharis" as water-lily water. The patient is "virgo" in the case, but the recipe's "sumat" has no gender; "her" is assumed.
translations.text: as camphor tied to the genitals and carried in the breeches (so one says) makes the member limp. A noble maiden suffered from this disease; among other things the physician prescribed that for twenty days she should wear on her back a leaden plate pierced with many holes; and to dry up the seed he ordered her to eat as sparingly as possible, and to eat often prepared coriander and the seed of lettuce and of sorrel; and so he freed her from the disease. Take of the seed of lettuce, purslane and coriander, of each 1 drachm, of dried mint ½ drachm, of the whitest sugar 4 ounces; let all be pounded finely, and afterward mix together with water-lily water, to make a solid confection in lozenges. Of these let her take one in the morning when she rises. Of innumerable things nearly like these, seek in Hildesheim at the place cited, Mizaldus, Porta, and the rest.

3.2.5.1-f47.text: ——— facilis descensus Averni; / Sed revocare gradum, superasque evadere ad auras; / Hic labor, hoc opus est. ——— / It is an easy passage down to hell, / But to come back, once there, you cannot well.

translations.literal: — easy the descent of Avernus; / but to recall the step and to escape out to the upper airs, / this the labour, this the work is. —
translations.note: The marked passage also contains Burton's own English couplet ('It is an easy passage down to hell, / But to come back, once there, you cannot well'), which loosely renders the Latin. Only the Latin is translated here. Because the couplet falls inside the marked passage, it is not quoted as a self-translation. Burton reads 'Averni'; modern editions print 'Averno', but 'Averni' is an ancient variant reading.
translations.text: — the descent to Avernus is easy; / but to retrace your step and escape to the upper air, / this is the task, this the toil. —

translations.note: The marked passage also contains Burton's own English couplet, which is not translated here. Burton's couplet is a loose rendering, but it lies inside the marked passage, so it is not quoted as a self-translation.
translations.text: ——— The descent to Avernus is easy; / but to retrace one's step and escape to the upper air, / this is the labour, this the task. ———
